explanation: Recall from Section 1.1: [[kw:real numbers]] ($\mathbb{R}$) are all numbers on the number line — rationals and irrationals.
The **properties of equality** hold for any real numbers $a, b, c$:
• [[kw:Reflexive Property]]: $a = a$.
• [[kw:Symmetric Property]]: If $a = b$, then $b = a$.
• [[kw:Transitive Property]]: If $a = b$ and $b = c$, then $a = c$.
A [[kw:binary operation]] combines two numbers to produce a third. Addition and multiplication are binary operations.

A set is **closed** under an operation if performing that operation on any two members always produces another member of the set. The real numbers are [[imp:closed under addition and multiplication]].
The [[kw:Substitution Principle]] says: if $a = b$, you can replace $a$ with $b$ in any expression.

notes: This means you'll never fall outside the real numbers when adding or multiplying.
Division by zero is not allowed, so closure under division requires a nonzero divisor.
formulaCard.title: Closure of $\mathbb{R}$
formulaCard.formula: $$ \text{If } a, b \in \mathbb{R}, \text{ then } a + b \in \mathbb{R} \text{ and } a \times b \in \mathbb{R} $$

explanation: The [[kw:additive identity]] is $0$: for any real $a$, $a + 0 = a$.
The [[kw:multiplicative identity]] is $1$: $a \times 1 = a$.
Every real number $a$ has an [[kw:additive inverse]] (opposite), written $-a$, such that $a + (-a) = 0$.
Every nonzero real number $a$ has a [[kw:multiplicative inverse]] (reciprocal), $a^{-1} = \frac{1}{a}$, such that $a \times a^{-1} = 1$.
[[imp:Zero has no multiplicative inverse]] — you cannot divide by zero.

notes: The additive inverse is also called the negative.
The multiplicative inverse is also called the reciprocal.

formulaCard.title: Absolute Value Definition

explanation: Every real number corresponds to exactly one point on the [[kw:number line]], and vice versa.
The [[kw:absolute value]] of a number $x$, written $|x|$, is its distance from $0$ on the number line. Distance is always nonnegative.
Formally: $|x| = x$ if $x \ge 0$, and $|x| = -x$ if $x < 0$.
Sign rules for addition: the sum of two positives is positive; sum of two negatives is negative; if opposite signs, the sign of the sum matches the addend with the larger absolute value.
Sign rules for multiplication/division: same signs → positive product/quotient; different signs → negative product/quotient.

teacherCues: Draw a number line from -10 to 10. Mark points and ask: 'What is the absolute value of -7?'
Write 'positive × negative = ?' and use patterns like -2 × 3 = -6 to deduce the rule.

discoveryHook.scenario: Think of the number line as a city street — zero is home. Positive numbers are steps east; negatives are steps west. Absolute value is just how far you are from home, no matter the direction. And when you multiply, signs follow a simple dance: two positives or two negatives make a positive, while opposite signs make negative!

formulaCard.formula: $$ a(b + c) = ab + ac \quad \text{and} \quad (b + c)a = ba + ca $$
formulaCard.title: Distributive Law in Detail

explanation: The [[kw:Commutative Laws]] state that order doesn't matter for addition and multiplication: $a + b = b + a$ and $a \times b = b \times a$.
The [[kw:Associative Laws]] state that grouping doesn't matter: $(a + b) + c = a + (b + c)$ and $(ab)c = a(bc)$.
The [[kw:Distributive Law]] connects multiplication and addition: $a(b + c) = ab + ac$. It works both ways — expanding and factoring.
These laws are the backbone of simplifying expressions and solving equations throughout Algebra I.

discoveryHook.scenario: Without a universal order of operations, math would be chaos — different answers for the same problem! The blueprint ensures everyone arrives at the same result. And when you're asked to 'justify your steps,' you're simply naming which axiom of real numbers gives you permission to take each step.

examples.title: Example A — Simple PEMDAS
steps: **Understand:** The expression has subtraction, multiplication, addition, and an exponent.
**Solve:** Exponent first: $4^2 = 16$ → $10 - 2 \times 3 + 16$. Multiply: $2 \times 3 = 6$ → $10 - 6 + 16$. Add/Subtract left to right: $4 + 16 = 20$.

Explain to a partner: Why must you start with the innermost parentheses $(3^2 - 1)$ before the brackets $[\;]$?
examples.title: Example B — Nested Grouping Symbols
steps: **Understand:** Expression has brackets, parentheses, exponent, multiplication, division.
**Solve:** Innermost: $3^2 = 9$, then $9 - 1 = 8$. Now bracket: $5 + 8 = 13$. Expression becomes $2 \times 13 \div 4 = 26 \div 4 = 6.5$.

examples.title: Example C — Justify with Axioms
steps: **Solve:** $(x + 2) - x = (x + 2) + (-x)$ (definition of subtraction). $= (2 + x) + (-x)$ (commutative of addition). $= 2 + (x + (-x))$ (associative). $= 2 + 0 = 2$ (inverse and identity).
examples.prompt: Simplify $ (x + 2) - x $ and justify each step with an axiom.

confusionCorner.body: When you have only multiplication and division, or only addition and subtraction, go left to right. For example, $10 \div 2 \times 5$: do $10 \div 2 = 5$, then $5 \times 5 = 25$. [[imp:Not $2 \times 5$ first!]]
confusionCorner.title: Left‑to‑Right Trap

blocks.title: Blueprint: Order of Operations & Justifying with Axioms

explanation: The **Understand → Solve → Conclude** blueprint breaks down complex simplifications:
[[imp:Understand:]] Identify the expression, and note which operations and grouping symbols are present.

[[imp:Solve:]] Apply the order of operations (PEMDAS): 1) grouping symbols innermost first, 2) exponents, 3) multiplication/division left to right, 4) addition/subtraction left to right. Use real‑number axioms to justify each simplification.
[[imp:Conclude:]] Write the final simplified result, and if applicable, state the axiom used in the last step.
The real number axioms include closure, identity, inverse, commutative, associative, and distributive properties — they are your tools for justifying every move.

formulaCard.title: Blueprint Summary
notes: Always work inside‑out for nested parentheses.
Multiplication and division are equal in priority; do them left‑to‑right.

teacherCues: Write a complex expression like $3 + 4 \times 2^2 \div (1+1)$ and ask: 'Which step comes first? Why?'
